prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks, in which neutral atoms trapped at a magic wavelength enable measurement of time and frequency at the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: After the first round my preferred configuration is unchanged: a single-part prize for optical lattice clocks to Hidetoshi Katori and Jun Ye. I want to say plainly that seven of eight files agreeing is not my argument, and that several colleagues reached B004 by moving from other first choices, so I have tried to test the case again from the instrument-builder's side. The decisive point is that the magic-wavelength lattice is a separate idea from the comb and from single-ion control. The comb counts optical cycles, and ion clocks reach their accuracy by isolating one particle and accepting a poor signal-to-noise ratio. The lattice removes Doppler, recoil and light-shift limits while interrogating thousands of atoms at once, which converts a statistical advantage into an accuracy advantage. That is why the field went from the 1e-15 range to about 1e-18 within roughly fifteen years. Katori proposed the lattice and made the first strontium lattice clock. Ye's group then took the systematic uncertainty and stability to the frontier and added the many-body, Fermi-degenerate clock and the comb-clock integration. Independent reproduction at RIKEN, JILA/NIST, PTB, SYRTE and other laboratories, with intercontinental comparisons that agree, answers my standing question about independent confirmation. The physics will last, because any future definition of the second or any test of constants and redshift will be built on this technique. I would word the citation so that the lattice itself is the subject, as Danielsson asked, and I would justify it by capability and by the new regime of measurement, not by any claim about constants, since those tests have so far returned null results. I keep a two-name credit: neither the record nor any colleague has shown a third contribution of the same decisive kind.
statement.case_against: The overlap with the 2005 frequency-comb prize and the 2012 prize for control of single quantum systems and ion clocks remains the strongest objection, and wording will decide whether it bites. The prize is for a measurement tool and not a surprise in nature, so a sceptic can call it a refinement of precision spectroscopy. The redefinition of the SI second has not happened, so part of the payoff is prospective. Attribution is imperfect, since Lemonde, Takamoto, Hinkley, Ludlow, Oates and the SYRTE group sit outside two names, and Ye appears in other candidacies. I also acknowledge that I am an astroparticle experimentalist and not an atomic physicist, so the priority question between Katori's proposal and the first operational clock, and the exact weight of the ion-clock lineage, are points where I rely on Lindroth, Olsson and Kroll. Finally, I am chairing and I know that a chair who sees a convergence can mistake it for evidence, so I have deliberately kept the argument scientific.

responses.point: Danielsson moved B004 from eighth to first, says the lattice itself is not contained in the comb, but says the counts alone must not be the argument and that B004 is an instrument achievement and not a new phenomenon.
responses.response: I agree that the lattice is not contained in the comb, and I would adopt your wording request, so the citation names the magic-wavelength lattice and neutral atoms explicitly. On your last point, I would not defend the prize by the constants tests. The limits are null so far, and I would be uncomfortable if the Academy implied a discovery that has not been made. The defensible claim is capability: a regime of precision that did not exist, reproduced independently. I also thank you for the point on B045. I accept your reading that your cosmology preference was a bias to discount, and that a BAO prize would need a clean separation from the 2011 and 2019 cosmology prizes, which is why I still do not support it.

responses.point: Eriksson keeps B010 first on the theory-then-experiment structure, but concedes the field is about eight years old, the pairing mechanism is open, Yuan Cao is outside the trio, and a maturity-first reading could put B004 ahead.
responses.response: You make the best case for B010 and I do not dismiss it: a quantitative prediction in 2011 and an experimental answer in 2018 is the structure I respect. The attribution is the problem I cannot resolve, because Cao is first author on the decisive papers and Lopes dos Santos, Peres, Castro Neto and Suarez Morell are outside the trio, and eight years is short for a result I would call lasting. You asked what must be true for it to rank beside B004. For me the answer is time, and a settled account of who made the decisive contribution. I keep B010 as an alternative. You also say you defer to AMO colleagues on the overlap with 2005 and 2012. As chair I note that Lindroth, Olsson and Kroll, who know the atomic physics, each rank B004 first and each state the overlap as the main reservation, so I do not think this is a case where the experts disagree on priority. If you accept their account, I would hope you can accept B004 for the final vote, but I would not ask you to give up B010 on my account.

responses.point: Olsson asks whether Katori's magic-wavelength proposal or the first operational clock is the original contribution, and says the pending SI redefinition could sharpen the citation.
responses.response: I think the citation should avoid forcing that choice, which is why I keep both words, invention and realisation. The proposal alone would not have changed the field, and the realisation alone would not have been possible without the proposal, so both are in Katori's name, and Ye's contribution is the performance frontier and the many-body clock. On the SI second, I agree it could sharpen the wording, but I do not accept that we should wait. If the redefinition arrives we would then be rewarding a decision taken by metrology bodies, where today we reward the measurement that made the decision possible. I would, however, like the secretariat to check priority details with external AMO experts before the final wording.

responses.point: Mehlig moved from B007 to B004 but still sees a risk that lattice clocks are a refinement of established precision spectroscopy and that a two-name prize leaves out Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow and Oates.
responses.response: I think the refinement reading fails on the physics: the lattice changes the error budget, because it permits Doppler-free and recoil-free interrogation of thousands of atoms, which the ion route cannot do. A refinement would improve the same instrument, and this is a different one. On names, I would put the question back to the committee in the form I put it in the summary: a third name needs a specific decisive contribution that is separable from the pair, and nobody has stated one. Lemonde and Takamoto made important contributions, but important is not the same as decisive, and a shared prize that goes to three of five or six strong contributors is no fairer than two with a clear division of roles. I would add that your opening B007 case remains a good one for a later year, and I would not want your move to B004 to be read as a rejection of it.

responses.point: Kroll values the credit coherence of a single-topic prize and asks whether a two-part prize pairing the clock with a quantum-technology topic would be worth the loss of coherence.
responses.response: My answer is no. A second part would have to stand on its own, and none of the alternatives is ready. B034 follows the 2025 prize on superconducting circuits and has an unresolved choice among four names, B010 has the Cao problem, and I will not propose B032 because of my own field proximity and because the source associations are still at modest significance. B036 is the nearest to a good second part, since atom interferometry is a reproduced measurement technique with a clear lineage, but it would sit beside B004 as another precision-measurement prize, and a two-part prize with two metrology parts is not more informative than one good prize. I agree with you that the coherence of the single prize is worth protecting.

uncertainties: Whether the final citation wording is enough to separate lattice clocks from the 2005 frequency-comb and 2012 single-quantum-system prizes; I think so, but I am not an atomic physicist and rely on Lindroth, Olsson and Kroll.

Whether the original contribution of Katori is best expressed as proposal, first demonstration, or both, and whether outside AMO experts would place Lemonde or Takamoto on the same footing as the pair.
Whether the SI second redefinition happening or not happening in the next few years changes how timely the award appears.
Whether a later cycle will see B010 resolve its attribution and mechanism questions, and whether B036 would then be a better companion than a second part now.
statement.conflict_note: No conflict with Katori, Ye or their collaborations; my collaborations are PAMELA, Fermi-LAT and XL-Calibur. I keep my field-proximity disclosure for B032 IceCube (same astroparticle community, not in the collaboration), and I am not proposing it. As chair I note that Johansson has flagged B034 and B043, Kroll has disclosed a mild overlap with quantum-technology candidates, and none of these touches the preferred configuration, so I do not see a need for a formal recusal on B004. I have no apparent connection to the persons credited on the other shortlisted candidates.
